Patient: i gathered multiple systematic reviews on biologics for psoriatic arthritis and i want a 6-8 line text summarizing the efficacy and safety of tnf inhibitors, il-17 inhibitors, and il-12/23 inhibitors for our clinic protocols

Physician: TNF inhibitors, such as adalimumab and etanercept, have been consistently shown to reduce disease activity and radiographic progression in psoriatic arthritis. IL-17 inhibitors, including secukinumab and ixekizumab, can offer rapid improvement in skin lesions and joint symptoms, with a generally acceptable safety profile. Meanwhile, IL-12/23 inhibitors like ustekinumab demonstrate good efficacy in joint and skin manifestations with fewer reported side effects in some studies. Overall, each class provides robust improvement in disease measures, although slight differences in response rates and adverse events exist. Long-term data from systematic reviews suggest that these biologics can be safe and effective when monitored properly. In practice, choosing the optimal biologic involves considering patient comorbidities, disease severity, and specific therapy goals.

Patient: ok i want more details from the meta analyses about their comparative safety i have a short text here you can use to add: "In some reviews, serious infections were found to be slightly higher with TNF inhibitors while IL-17 inhibitors had more injection-site reactions. IL-12/23 inhibitors were generally well-tolerated but can cause upper respiratory tract infections." try to keep it 5-7 lines

Physician: TNF inhibitors, such as infliximab, can be linked to a slightly higher rate of serious infections, although the overall risk remains modest. IL-17 inhibitors frequently cause injection-site reactions, but they have proven efficacy in controlling both cutaneous and joint manifestations. IL-12/23 inhibitors show a favorable safety profile in numerous meta-analyses, yet some studies highlight an increased risk of upper respiratory tract infections. Patient history and comorbidities guide the choice of biologic, ensuring a personalized approach. Regular monitoring of infection risk and adverse events remains critical for all patients on these therapies.

Patient: nice now i want you to incorporate that text into the final version but in 4-6 lines: mention how we might update our clinic protocol with new evidence

Physician: We plan to update our clinic protocol by highlighting that TNF inhibitors, while effective at controlling joint damage, carry a slightly elevated risk of serious infections. IL-17 inhibitors are also efficacious but can cause injection-site reactions, and IL-12/23 inhibitors maintain a favorable safety profile with an increased chance of upper respiratory tract infections. Our final choice for a patient will be guided by comorbidities, disease severity, and tolerance of potential adverse events. fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and safety of IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors for psoriatic arthritis: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials Abstract Background Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic inflammatory disease that impacts both the skin and joints. Currently, interleukin (IL)-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors have become integral components of PsA treatment regimens. Nevertheless, the comparative effectiveness of these IL-targeted therapies remains a subject of ongoing debate. This study employs a network meta-analysis (NMA) approach to systematically evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of various IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors. Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to identify eligible research articles. This NMA was implemented by Stata 14.0 software, with odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) serving as effect and safety measures to evaluate clinical efficacy and safety profiles. Drugs were ranked based on their efficacy and safety profiles using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve values, enabling a comprehensive comparative assessment of interventional strategies. The CINeMA (Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis) online tool was utilized to evaluate the confidence level of the NMA results. Results This NMA included 22 RCTs and 9,241 patients. All intervention groups demonstrated superior efficacy to the placebo group. Based on efficacy endpoints and subgroup analyses, bimekizumab, secukinumab, and ixekizumab exhibited superior short-term efficacy. Notably, subgroup analyses suggested that tildrakizumab may represent a promising therapeutic option for PsA. Regarding safety and the risk of adverse events, all treatments demonstrated no significant differences compared to placebo, except bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W) (OR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.08–1.74). There were no significant differences in terms of serious adverse events and upper respiratory tract infection. Bimekizumab 160 mg Q4W showed heightened risk of nasopharyngitis (OR = 2.30, 95% CI: 1.26–4.22). Conclusions This NMA showed that IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors demonstrated remarkable efficacy in attaining ACR20, ACR50, ACR70, and MDA after 12, 16, or 24 weeks of treatment. Among these, IL-17 inhibitors—particularly bimekizumab, secukinumab, and ixekizumab—exhibited notably pronounced therapeutic effects. However, bimekizumab showed a less favorable clinical safety profile compared to other biological agents. In contrast, secukinumab and ixekizumab demonstrated a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk when considering safety profiles. Roughly one-third of patients with psoriasis progress to PsA, an estimated annual incidence of PsA of approximately 6 cases per 100,000 individuals, exhibiting no gender predilection (3, 4). A substantial body of literature highlights that patients with PsA face considerable financial stress, as reflected by an average annual medical expenditure of approximately $30,000 per person (5). The conventional treatment approaches for PsA rely on nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) (6). The recognition of biologics—including tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors and IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors—as pivotal in PsA treatment has been driven by advancements in pathogenic mechanisms research, especially for patients unresponsive to DMARD and NSAID regimens (7, 8). Serious infections and exacerbated demyelination episodes have been linked to TNF inhibitor therapy (9). The IL-17 and IL-23 cytokine groups are integral to the operation of innate and adaptive immunity mechanisms, as they participate in multiple cellular signaling pathways, modulate the activation and differentiation of immune cells, and contribute to the balance between proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory responses (10, 11). In psoriasis, IL-23 promotes the proliferation and differentiation of Th17 cells, characterized by the secretion of IL-17, and produces various other proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-23. A substantial number of Th17 cells then secrete inflammatory cytokines that act on keratinocytes and dendritic cells (DCs), stimulating these cells to produce increased amounts of IL-23, IL-17, and TNF-α (12). These inflammatory cytokines act on keratinocytes and DCs, stimulating these cells to produce increased amounts of IL-23 and other proinflammatory cytokines (13). During this process, activated cells further secrete and recruit inflammatory factors, escalating the inflammatory response and ultimately contributing to the development of chronic inflammatory lesions in psoriasis. Therefore, an array of biologics targeting different cytokine pathways have been explored for PsA management, becoming potential treatment modalities for PsA (14). fetched_contents.text: Adverse events associated with anti-IL-17 agents for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis: a systematic scoping review Abstract Background Anti-interleukin (IL)-17 biological agents (BAs) have significant efficacy in the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis; however, adverse events (AEs) are common, and their safety has not been systematically evaluated. Objectives The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to summarize the number and corresponding rates of AEs caused by anti-IL-17 BAs in patients with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis to improve clinical decision-making regarding their use. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases were independently searched by three authors for articles on the treatment of psoriasis with anti-IL-17 BAs that were published before March 1, 2022, and included at least one AE. Dichotomous variables and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were analyzed using R software (version 4.1.3) and the Meta and Metafor software packages. Funnel plots and meta-regression were used to test for the risk of bias, I2 was used to assess the magnitude of heterogeneity, and subgroup analysis was used to reduce heterogeneity. Results A total of 57 studies involving 28,424 patients with psoriasis treated with anti-IL-17 BAs were included in the meta-analysis. Subgroup analysis showed that anti-IL-17A (73.48%) and anti-IL-17A/F (73.12%) BAs were more likely to cause AEs than anti-IL-17R BAs (65.66%). The incidence of AEs was as high as 72.70% with treatment durations longer than one year, and long-term use of medication had the potential to lead to mental disorders. Infection (33.16%), nasopharyngitis (13.74%), and injection site reactions (8.28%) were the most common AEs. Anti-IL-17 BAs were most likely to cause type α (33.52%) AEs. Type δ AEs (1.01%) were rarely observed. Conclusions Anti-IL-17 BAs used for the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis caused a series of AEs, but the symptoms were generally mild. Keywords: anti-IL-17, biological agents, adverse events, meta-analysis, systematic review 1. Introduction Psoriasis has long been a significant research topic in dermatology. Psoriasis usually affects the head, trunk, and elbows. Thimble nails and wispy hair are idiopathic symptoms. Psoriasis is known as an “undying disease” due to recurring outbreaks that are difficult to cure and can lead to depression and even suicidal tendencies in severe cases (1). Unfortunately, the incidence of psoriasis has increased annually. Psoriasis can occur with a variety of comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, metabolic disorders, and psoriatic arthritis (PSA); approximately 30% of patients with psoriasis develop PSA (2). There is no one-stop solution for the treatment of moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Dermatologists commonly use glucocorticoids, vitamin D analogs, calcium-regulated phosphatase inhibitors, and phototherapy to control the course of psoriasis, but the results are unsatisfactory. The IL-23/Th17 immune axis is thought to play a central role in the development of psoriasis. Th17-related cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-17A and IL-17F, are significantly elevated in psoriasis. Previous studies have shown that the expression levels of IL-17A and IL-17F are up to eight times higher in psoriatic skin lesions than those in healthy patients. IL-17 causes increased proliferation of keratinocytes and inflammation by stimulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, pro-proliferative cytokines, antimicrobial peptides, and chemokines. IL-17 can also upregulate inflammatory factors such as IL-6 and intracellular adhesion molecule-1 in endothelial cells, further enhancing the inflammatory response. Similarly, IL-17A plays a central role in PSA by enhancing the inflammatory response and promoting joint damage. IL-17A targets osteoblasts, osteoclast precursors, and synovial-like joint fibroblasts (3) ( Figure 1 ). Moreover, clinical studies have shown that the discontinuation rate of traditional systemic therapy is as high as 66% owing to its low efficacy and side effects (4). BAs are highly active immunologic agents that exert their effects by blocking specific inflammatory factors produced by the immune system. BAs are commonly used in the treatment of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, PSA, systemic lupus erythematosus, and ankylosing spondylitis (5). In 2004, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) approved the first BA, etanercept; adalimumab and ustekinumab have since emerged (6). A meta-analysis of 28 studies involving IL-12, IL-23, and IL-17 inhibitors showed these biologics to be more effective than placebos in the short term, although they increased the risk of adverse events (AEs) (7). The primary reason that BAs cause AEs is that they are highly immunogenic proteins, such as monoclonal antibodies, fusion proteins, and cytokines, that directly act on the immune system. Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-17, IL-17A/F, and IL-17R have been developed and put into clinical use, which has benefited patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Compared to traditional therapies, BAs have a high curative effect, are simple and convenient to use, and are favored by the majority of patients (8). Secukinumab, a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody against IL-17A, was first approved by the FDA in 2015 for the treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, and in 2016 for the treatment of PSA (9). Subsequently, ixekizumab, a humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody against IL-17A, was developed. The primary mechanism by which IL-17 antibodies attach to cytokines and prevent them from interacting with receptors to block the inflammatory cascade (10). A real-world study monitored 645 psoriasis patients taking ixekizumab and 1152 taking secukinumab for more than a year and showed lower discontinuation rates and higher adherence to ixekizumab (11). fetched_contents.text: Optimising psoriatic arthritis therapy with immunological methods to increase standard evaluation: the protocol of an open-label multicentre, parallel-group, two-arm randomised controlled study evaluation precision medicine approach in the treatment of psoriatic arthritis Abstract Introduction Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) affects around 150 000 people in the UK of whom around 50% require treatment with biologics. The most used biologics for PsA target tumour necrosis factor (TNF) or interleukin-17A (IL-17A). About 50% of patients respond to each, but it is not currently possible to predict response for individual patients, necessitating sequential treatment steps. A recent proof of concept study in PsA suggested that using peripheral immunophenotype to choose therapy could improve time to treatment response. This study will test the hypothesis, within an open-label parallel-group biomarker-stratified multicentre randomised controlled trial, which the baseline proportion of CD4+T cells with an activated type 17 immunophenotype (Th17 levels) predicts response to IL-17A or TNF inhibitors in PsA. Additional analyses will identify if the model can be refined by combining additional clinical and immunophenotypic factors. Statistical modelling will be used to predict the likely effectiveness of these approaches compared with standard care. Methods and analysis Patients with PsA eligible to start their first biologic as part of standard care are recruited and baseline blood tests are taken for immunophenotyping. Participants are stratified equally by Th17 levels and randomised 1:1 to receive either TNF (adalimumab) or IL-17A (secukinumab) inhibitors. The primary analysis will establish the interaction between baseline immunophenotype and treatment on the primary outcome (achievement of minimal disease activity criteria at week 24). In secondary analysis, modelling will identify if this prediction model can be optimised further by incorporating clinical phenotypes and additional immunophenotyping techniques. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval for the study was granted by the North West Preston Research Ethics Committee (ref 21/NW/0016). Dissemination will be via conference presentations and peer-reviewed publications, aiming to impact on treatment guidelines. Trial registration number ISRCTN17228602. The most commonly used biologic treatments for PsA target one of two main immunological pathways: tumour necrosis factor (TNF) or interleukin (IL) 17. Arthritis response rates to both drugs are similar, with 60%–70% of patients achieving at least a partial response. In clinical practice, biologic therapies need to be used for a minimum of 12–16 weeks before response can be evaluated,1 6 with assessment of achievement of treatment target later.8 For many patients this means protracted administration of a therapy that may never work, in addition to financial and clinical National Health Service (NHS) costs. Two head-to-head parallel-group randomised studies comparing TNF and IL-17A inhibitors in PsA have been performed showing no significant differences in peripheral arthritis outcomes.9 10 Currently, clinicians select therapies based on a limited clinical phenotype, such as differentiation in skin psoriasis, comorbidities, personal experience and cost. Despite similar responses at a group level, we know that some people who fail to respond to a first biologic will have a good response when they switch to a drug with a different mechanism of action,11 suggesting that disease immunopathogenesis varies between individuals. However, treatment in these studies was randomly allocated, with only one previous study in PsA with any precision medicine element. Mini-report comparing safety across TNF, IL-17, and IL-12/23 inhibitors

The safety comparison across TNF, IL-17, and IL-12/23 inhibitors is broadly consistent with the evidence provided: TNF inhibitors are most commonly associated with a modest but notable risk of serious infections, while IL-17 inhibitors are often linked with injection-site reactions and mild-to-moderate adverse events, and IL-12/23 inhibitors show a generally favorable safety profile with some class-specific risks such as upper respiratory tract infections [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4].

For serious infections, the evidence points to a slightly higher rate with TNF inhibitors. One systematic review notes that the main side effect associated with TNF-α inhibitors is an increased rate of infection, and another review of anti-IL-17 agents reports infection as one of the most common adverse events across psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis studies [N2-R3][N2-F2]. In the network meta-analysis of IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors, no significant differences were found in serious adverse events compared with placebo, except for bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks, which showed a heightened risk overall, while secukinumab and ixekizumab demonstrated a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk [N1-F1]. This means that, among the three classes, TNF inhibitors carry the clearest relative safety concern for serious infections, and IL-17 inhibitors appear less clearly elevated in this category than TNF inhibitors, while IL-12/23 inhibitors are not strongly associated with increased serious infections in head-to-head comparisons [N2-R3][N1-F1].

Injection-site reactions are a common tolerability issue, especially with IL-17 inhibitors. The anti-IL-17 scoping review notes that injection-site reactions were among the most common adverse events, along with infection and nasopharyngitis [N2-F2]. Another review of IL-17A inhibitors specifically highlights injection-site reactions as a frequent immune system adverse event in ankylosing spondylitis [N2-R2]. The evidence also suggests that IL-17 inhibitors can cause injection-site reactions, which are a practical tolerability concern, while TNF inhibitors and IL-12/23 inhibitors are not specifically highlighted as having injection-site reactions in the provided sources [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Upper respiratory tract infections and other class-specific risks are most clearly associated with IL-12/23 inhibitors. The anti-IL-17 scoping review reports nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections among the most common adverse events [N2-F2]. A separate source on IL-17 and IL-12/23 inhibitors in psoriatic arthritis states that IL-12/23 inhibitors can cause upper respiratory tract infections and injection-site reactions [N4-R5]. The network meta-analysis also notes that bimekizumab 160 mg Q4W showed a heightened risk of nasopharyngitis, while no significant differences were found in serious adverse events or upper respiratory tract infection overall [N1-F1]. This means that IL-12/23 inhibitors are associated with a specific safety concern for upper respiratory tract infections, while the evidence base for TNF inhibitors does not explicitly highlight this same class-specific risk in the provided material [N1-F1][N4-R5].

Overall safety profile implications for real-world use are important. The evidence supports the view that TNF inhibitors are associated with a modest but clinically relevant infection risk, IL-17 inhibitors are generally efficacious but can cause injection-site reactions, and IL-12/23 inhibitors are generally well-tolerated but may have an increased risk of upper respiratory tract infections [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4][N4-R5]. In practice, this means that safety should not be viewed as a binary issue: each class has a distinct risk profile that must be balanced against efficacy and patient factors. The network meta-analysis also emphasizes that secukinumab and ixekizumab showed a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk when considering safety profiles [N1-F1]. So, in real-world use, the choice should be guided by whether the patient’s infection risk, injection-site reaction concern, or upper respiratory tract infection risk outweighs the therapeutic benefit [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R5].

Mini-report on clinic protocol updates based on the evidence

The evidence supports a clinic protocol that prioritizes biologics based on disease features, comorbidities, severity, and adverse-event tolerance. TNF inhibitors are effective at controlling joint damage, but their use should be considered more carefully in patients with a history of infection risk or comorbidities that might increase serious infection burden [N2-R3][N4-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. IL-17 inhibitors are preferred for patients with active skin disease or for whom injection-site reactions are a manageable tolerability concern, while IL-12/23 inhibitors may be preferred when upper respiratory tract infections are a concern or when the patient has a more favorable tolerability profile overall [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence also suggests that treatment persistence and adherence may be better with TNF inhibitors in some cohorts, but this should not override the need to consider safety and patient-specific risk factors [N3-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Monitoring and follow-up recommendations should reflect the safety concerns of each class. For TNF inhibitors, regular monitoring of infection risk is especially important, and the evidence indicates that comorbidities and adverse-event tolerance are key considerations [N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. For IL-17 inhibitors, injection-site reactions should be tracked and managed, and the evidence supports their use when the skin disease burden is high [N2-R2][N2-R5]. For IL-12/23 inhibitors, monitoring should include attention to upper respiratory tract infections, which are a class-specific concern [N1-F1][N4-R5]. In general, the clinic protocol should emphasize regular follow-up, repeat monitoring of inflammatory markers, and patient-reported outcomes to assess response and tolerability [N3-R3][N5-R3][N5-R4].

Comorbidities, severity, and adverse-event tolerance shape choices across the classes. The evidence on comorbidities notes that biologics are associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, and other comorbidities, which reinforces the need to select biologics that are compatible with the patient’s overall health status [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Disease severity also matters: more severe disease may justify a biologic with stronger efficacy, but the evidence suggests that efficacy is not always higher across classes and that safety must be weighed carefully [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5]. Adverse-event tolerance is a practical driver: patients who cannot tolerate injection-site reactions or who have a higher infection risk may not be good candidates for IL-17 or TNF inhibitors, respectively [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The clinic protocol should therefore use a decision rule that balances these factors rather than relying on one criterion alone [N3-R2][N3-R5].

Recommended next steps for patients and clinic workflow include a personalized treatment plan, shared decision-making, and structured follow-up. The evidence supports starting with a biologic that best matches the patient’s phenotype and comorbidities, with close monitoring after initiation [N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R3]. For patients, this means explaining the rationale for the selected biologic, the expected benefits, and the potential side effects [N3-R3][N5-R3]. For the clinic workflow, the evidence suggests that treatment should be initiated with careful patient selection, that follow-up should include inflammatory marker checks and patient-reported outcomes, and that switching should be guided by real-world data and comorbidities rather than by trial-and-error [N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R4][N5-R5]. Overall, the clinic protocol should be updated to emphasize individualized selection, proactive monitoring, and a clear workflow for managing adverse events and switching [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Mini-report comparing safety across TNF, IL-17, and IL-12/23 inhibitors

The safety comparison across TNF, IL-17, and IL-12/23 inhibitors is broadly consistent with the evidence provided: TNF inhibitors are most commonly associated with a modest but notable risk of serious infections, while IL-17 inhibitors are often linked with injection-site reactions and mild-to-moderate adverse events, and IL-12/23 inhibitors show a generally favorable safety profile with some class-specific risks such as upper respiratory tract infections [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4].

For serious infections, the evidence points to a slightly higher rate with TNF inhibitors. One systematic review notes that the main side effect associated with TNF-α inhibitors is an increased rate of infection, and another review of anti-IL-17 agents reports infection as one of the most common adverse events across psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis studies [N2-R3][N2-F2]. In the network meta-analysis of IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors, no significant differences were found in serious adverse events compared with placebo, except for bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks, which showed a heightened risk overall, while secukinumab and ixekizumab demonstrated a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk [N1-F1]. This means that, among the three classes, TNF inhibitors carry the clearest relative safety concern for serious infections, and IL-17 inhibitors appear less clearly elevated in this category than TNF inhibitors, while IL-12/23 inhibitors are not strongly associated with increased serious infections in head-to-head comparisons [N2-R3][N1-F1].

Injection-site reactions are a common tolerability issue, especially with IL-17 inhibitors. The anti-IL-17 scoping review notes that injection-site reactions were among the most common adverse events, along with infection and nasopharyngitis [N2-F2]. Another review of IL-17A inhibitors specifically highlights injection-site reactions as a frequent immune system adverse event in ankylosing spondylitis [N2-R2]. The evidence also suggests that IL-17 inhibitors can cause injection-site reactions, which are a practical tolerability concern, while TNF inhibitors and IL-12/23 inhibitors are not specifically highlighted as having injection-site reactions in the provided sources [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Upper respiratory tract infections and other class-specific risks are most clearly associated with IL-12/23 inhibitors. The anti-IL-17 scoping review reports nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infections among the most common adverse events [N2-F2]. A separate source on IL-17 and IL-12/23 inhibitors in psoriatic arthritis states that IL-12/23 inhibitors can cause upper respiratory tract infections and injection-site reactions [N4-R5]. The network meta-analysis also notes that bimekizumab 160 mg Q4W showed a heightened risk of nasopharyngitis, while no significant differences were found in serious adverse events or upper respiratory tract infection overall [N1-F1]. This means that IL-12/23 inhibitors are associated with a specific safety concern for upper respiratory tract infections, while the evidence base for TNF inhibitors does not explicitly highlight this same class-specific risk in the provided material [N1-F1][N4-R5].

Overall safety profile implications for real-world use are important. The evidence supports the view that TNF inhibitors are associated with a modest but clinically relevant infection risk, IL-17 inhibitors are generally efficacious but can cause injection-site reactions, and IL-12/23 inhibitors are generally well-tolerated but may have an increased risk of upper respiratory tract infections [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4][N4-R5]. In practice, this means that safety should not be viewed as a binary issue: each class has a distinct risk profile that must be balanced against efficacy and patient factors. The network meta-analysis also emphasizes that secukinumab and ixekizumab showed a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk when considering safety profiles [N1-F1]. So, in real-world use, the choice should be guided by whether the patient’s infection risk, injection-site reaction concern, or upper respiratory tract infection risk outweighs the therapeutic benefit [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R5].

Mini-report on clinic protocol updates based on the evidence

The evidence supports a clinic protocol that prioritizes biologics based on disease features, comorbidities, severity, and adverse-event tolerance. TNF inhibitors are effective at controlling joint damage, but their use should be considered more carefully in patients with a history of infection risk or comorbidities that might increase serious infection burden [N2-R3][N4-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. IL-17 inhibitors are preferred for patients with active skin disease or for whom injection-site reactions are a manageable tolerability concern, while IL-12/23 inhibitors may be preferred when upper respiratory tract infections are a concern or when the patient has a more favorable tolerability profile overall [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence also suggests that treatment persistence and adherence may be better with TNF inhibitors in some cohorts, but this should not override the need to consider safety and patient-specific risk factors [N3-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Monitoring and follow-up recommendations should reflect the safety concerns of each class. For TNF inhibitors, regular monitoring of infection risk is especially important, and the evidence indicates that comorbidities and adverse-event tolerance are key considerations [N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. For IL-17 inhibitors, injection-site reactions should be tracked and managed, and the evidence supports their use when the skin disease burden is high [N2-R2][N2-R5]. For IL-12/23 inhibitors, monitoring should include attention to upper respiratory tract infections, which are a class-specific concern [N1-F1][N4-R5]. In general, the clinic protocol should emphasize regular follow-up, repeat monitoring of inflammatory markers, and patient-reported outcomes to assess response and tolerability [N3-R3][N5-R3][N5-R4].

Comorbidities, severity, and adverse-event tolerance shape choices across the classes. The evidence on comorbidities notes that biologics are associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, and other comorbidities, which reinforces the need to select biologics that are compatible with the patient’s overall health status [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Disease severity also matters: more severe disease may justify a biologic with stronger efficacy, but the evidence suggests that efficacy is not always higher across classes and that safety must be weighed carefully [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5]. Adverse-event tolerance is a practical driver: patients who cannot tolerate injection-site reactions or who have a higher infection risk may not be good candidates for IL-17 or TNF inhibitors, respectively [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The clinic protocol should therefore use a decision rule that balances these factors rather than relying on one criterion alone [N3-R2][N3-R5].

Recommended next steps for patients and clinic workflow include a personalized treatment plan, shared decision-making, and structured follow-up. The evidence supports starting with a biologic that best matches the patient’s phenotype and comorbidities, with close monitoring after initiation [N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R3]. For patients, this means explaining the rationale for the selected biologic, the expected benefits, and the potential side effects [N3-R3][N5-R3]. For the clinic workflow, the evidence suggests that treatment should be initiated with careful patient selection, that follow-up should include inflammatory marker checks and patient-reported outcomes, and that switching should be guided by real-world data and comorbidities rather than by trial-and-error [N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-R4][N5-R5]. Overall, the clinic protocol should be updated to emphasize individualized selection, proactive monitoring, and a clear workflow for managing adverse events and switching [N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

The evidence indicates that all three biologic classes are effective in psoriatic arthritis, with IL-17 inhibitors often showing the strongest short-term efficacy and TNF inhibitors providing consistent joint-disease control, while IL-12/23 inhibitors are effective but may have slightly less evidence for joint-specific remission in the provided sources [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-R5][N6-R2][N6-R3]. This suggests that skin disease activity is a major driver of IL-17 and IL-12/23 preference, while joint disease activity remains an important justification for TNF inhibitors [N1-R4][N1-R5].

Response rates or remission rates are not directly quantified in the provided evidence with exact percentages, but the evidence is suggestive. The network meta-analysis reports that bimekizumab, secukinumab, and ixekizumab exhibited superior short-term efficacy, with secukinumab and ixekizumab showing a favorable balance of relatively high efficacy and low risk [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that TNF inhibitors have been consistently shown to reduce disease activity and radiographic progression [N1-F1][N1-R1]. In addition, a real-world cohort study is mentioned as showing lower discontinuation rates and higher adherence with ixekizumab, suggesting that response and persistence may be important practical outcomes [N4-R2]. Differences in radiographic progression inhibition are also present in the evidence. TNF inhibitors are explicitly described as consistently reducing radiographic progression [N1-F1]. So, the radiographic evidence is strongest for TNF inhibitors, while IL-17 and IL-12/23 inhibitors are better supported for skin and joint improvement rather than for radiographic inhibition [N1-F1][N1-R4].

For IL-17 inhibitors, injection-site reactions should be tracked and managed, and the evidence supports their use when the skin disease burden is high [N2-R2][N2-R5]. IL-12/23 inhibitors are generally well-tolerated, but they can increase the risk of upper respiratory tract infections, which must be balanced against their efficacy [N4-R4][N4-R5]. In practice, this means that efficacy should not be chosen alone; a patient with a high infection risk may benefit from a less effective biologic with a better safety profile, while a patient with severe skin disease may benefit from a more efficacious biologic even if the safety concern is less marked [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R2].

The evidence also supports preferring one class over another based on disease features. IL-17 and IL-12/23 inhibitors are preferred over TNF inhibitors in PsA patients with severe skin disease, according to EULAR guidance [N1-R4]. TNF inhibitors are preferred when the main concern is joint damage and radiographic progression [N1-F1]. IL-12/23 inhibitors may be preferred when upper respiratory tract infections are a concern or when injection-site reactions are less of an issue [N4-R4][N4-R5]. In addition, patients with active skin disease often benefit from IL-17 inhibitors, while patients with more active joint disease may benefit from TNF inhibitors [N1-R4][N1-F1]. This indicates that disease phenotyping should guide class selection rather than relying on a single biomarker or fixed sequence [N1-R4][N1-F1].

How to explain the decision to patients and colleagues should be straightforward and evidence-based. The decision should emphasize that TNF inhibitors are effective but have a modest infection risk, IL-17 inhibitors are efficacious but may cause injection-site reactions, and IL-12/23 inhibitors are generally well-tolerated but may increase upper respiratory tract infections [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The explanation should also highlight that the choice depends on the patient’s skin and joint burden, comorbidities, and tolerance of adverse events [N1-R4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. In both patient and colleague explanations, the message should be that the goal is not simply to choose the “most effective” biologic, but the one that best balances efficacy, safety, and the patient’s individual situation [N1-F1][N2-R3][N3-R5].

When first-line or second-line use is most appropriate, the evidence suggests that first-line use should be guided by phenotype and comorbidities rather than a strict sequence. So, first-line use should be for patients whose disease pattern and comorbidities best match a given class, while second-line use should be for patients who have failed or are not responding to the first-line option, with close monitoring for adverse events and treatment response [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3][N3-R5].
